clients.description:
The client directory and one client's profile. Clients register themselves and are never deleted — every ledger row and audit entry has to keep resolving to a name — so this module has no create and no delete.

`clients.edit` and `clients.email` are DELIBERATELY SEPARATE, and the split is a security boundary rather than tidiness. Correcting a misspelled surname is clerical work a support desk does daily. Changing the address an account signs in with is an account-takeover primitive: set it to your own, run a password reset, and the balance is yours. Granting the first must not silently grant the second, so the everyday role carries `clients.edit` alone and `clients.email` is handed to the few people who handle lockouts.

permissions.label: Assign / Unassign Tags on a Client
Change Many Clients at Once (bulk tagging)

admins.description: The administrator directory, invitations and role assignment. Separate from clients on purpose: one key used to open both lists, so granting somebody the client list also handed them the admin directory.

permissions.label: Invite an Administrator & Revoke an Invite
Rename an Administrator & Assign Their Role
Set Which Client Tags an Administrator Is Limited To
Email an Administrator a Password Reset Link

roles.description: Roles are the only source of access in this system — there is no role above another and no wildcard. Editing a role takes effect on the next request from every administrator holding it.

kyc.description: The review queue, the documents clients upload, and the dynamic field builder behind them. Reviewing and configuring are separate: a reviewer decides on submissions, an administrator decides what is asked for.

permissions.label: Hand Back a Submission Another Reviewer Holds
Correct Identity Details on an Approved Submission

wallets.description: Client holdings, opening a wallet, and manual credits. Crediting and closing are separate keys because adding money and removing an account are not one power — and a credit is a real ledger movement (§6), not an edit to a number.

permissions.label: Open a Wallet for a Client
Add Funds to a Client Wallet

withdrawals.description: Reviewing and paying out client withdrawal requests. Approve and settle are SEPARATE keys on purpose (R-5.4): approval says a payout may be released, settlement releases it. While both required the same permission, 'two people must be involved in a payout' was unexpressible — one admin could authorise their own instruction and pay it out in the same minute, with the audit log showing one name on both rows.

deposits.description: Reviewing deposits a client paid OUTSIDE the platform — OMT, a bank transfer, cash — and credited on the strength of a receipt they uploaded. Separate from wallets.credit on purpose: approving here is BOUNDED (the amount is the client's own declaration against a reference that reconciles to a bank line), while wallets.credit types any amount into any wallet. A deposit clerk needs the first and must not be handed the second. Approve and reject are separate keys for the R-5.4 reason: refusing a declaration moves no money, crediting one does.

permissions.label: Approve a Deposit & Credit the Wallet

transactions.description: The platform-wide money-movement list: every deposit, withdrawal and internal transfer, across every client, with the client named on each row. Its own key rather than `withdrawals.view` for the reason the ledger got `ledger.view`: granting payout review must not also hand over every client deposit and every partner transfer on the platform. Its own key rather than `ledger.view` because the two screens answer different questions — the ledger is the append-only accounting record under Audit & Reconciliation, while this list shows lifecycle states, client identity and payment rails, and coupling them would mean granting either screen always grants both.

trading.description: No longer read-only: the MT5 bridge is live, so the console can open an account on the broker's server and move its balance. The three write keys are separate because they are three different powers — opening an account costs nothing, crediting one is giving away money, and debiting one is taking it. An operator who onboards clients needs the first and neither of the others.

permissions.label: Open a Trading Account on MT5

ib.description:
Two objects share this module and the keys go one level deeper because of it: editing a LEVEL changes what every partner standing on it earns, while moving one partner between levels changes what one partner earns.

`ib.programs.*` were removed in migration 0112 with the commission catalogue they governed, and `ib.levels.*` are back in their place — the ladder is the surface that replaced the catalogue, which is the swap 0104 made in the other direction. Whoever held the programme keys was granted the level equivalent, because silently narrowing somebody’s access during a refactor is a privilege change nobody asked for.

permissions.label: Change a Partner's Level or Parent

tags.description: The tag vocabulary itself. Deleting a tag is a privilege change rather than a label edit — an administrator restricted to it loses that restriction, and an empty scope means unrestricted — so delete is its own key. Applying a tag TO a client is clients.tag.

links.description: Links an administrator hands out: a client who signs up through one arrives carrying the link's tags, so they land in that administrator's book. A tag is a territory, so creating a link is deciding who will see the clients it brings — your own links may carry only tags from your own territory; links.manage covers everyone's.

permissions.label: Create & Edit Your Own Sign-up Links
Create, Edit & Reassign Anyone's Sign-up Links

currencies.description: Its own module rather than a corner of settings: a currency is a money object, and granting somebody the support email address should not also let them delete one.

leverages.description: The leverage ladder a client may open a trading account on. Its own module rather than a corner of settings, for the reason currencies are: leverage is a RISK control and a regulatory answer, and granting somebody the support email address should not also let them withdraw 1:500. There is no separate 'withdraw' key — taking a rung off the menu is an edit (`enabled: false`), and it is the action an operator almost always wants, because deleting is refused while any account is trading at that ratio.

externallinks.description: The links the client portal shows in its sidebar — an economic calendar, a help centre, a Telegram channel. Its own module rather than a corner of settings, for the reason currencies and leverages are: whatever holds this key can put a destination of its choosing in front of every client on the platform, and that should not arrive attached to a grant somebody made about the support email address. No 'withdraw' key — taking a link off the client menu is an edit (`enabled: false`), which keeps its title, description and position for when it comes back; deleting is how a link goes away for good.

payments.description: How clients can put money in — the methods offered on the deposit screen, their instructions, and the account details money is sent to. No delete key: `payments.edit` deletes only a method NO transaction references (a typo, a test row); a used one is disabled rather than removed, because its deposits must keep naming it.

paymentproviders.description: The systems that move the money behind the methods: Rival, the desk itself, and each provider added after them. Their connection settings, secrets, environment (live or sandbox) and on/off switch, and what each last reported. Apart from `payments.*` on purpose: a provider's settings decide where every payment and payout instruction goes, and its secrets can move money, while a payment method only decides what clients are offered. `payments.providers.*` replaced the Rival tab's `settings.rival.*` (0168), and 0177 removed those keys.

apikeys.description: Machine credentials for the admin API. Grant create NARROWLY: a key is standing access with no login and no session lifetime, carrying whatever permissions its creator holds, so the power to issue one is close to the power to grant one.

settings.description: Operational settings: brand, support contacts, terminal download links, outbound mail and the security controls. A singleton, so there is no create and no delete. The SMTP keys gate the SCREEN — the system sends mail regardless of who holds them.

audit.description:
The record of who did what, the append-only ledger, and the reconciliation report. Read-only throughout — none of these screens writes anything, so none has a write key.

`ledger.view` is its OWN key rather than riding on `withdrawals.view`, which is what the endpoint used to require. The ledger holds six entry types — deposit, withdrawal, commission, rebate, payout and adjustment — and only one of them is a withdrawal, so gating it on the withdrawal queue handed anyone reviewing payouts every deposit and every partner commission on the platform. Reading every money movement is its own power, on the same reasoning that keeps `wallets.credit` apart from `wallets.delete`.
